L5: # Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
L6: 
L7: Oct 15
L8: 
L9: Written by 【1†Jan Wehner】
L10: 
L11: This report was coauthored by Jam Kraprayoon.
L12: 
L13: 【2†Read the Full Report】
L14: AI agents are now being deployed at scale inside many organizations, spanning frontier AI companies, other enterprises, and government agencies. These agents are often entrusted to write code, manage infrastructure, and handle sensitive information, which has opened up a novel kind of insider risk. Much like human insider threats, these systems can use their legitimate insider access to damage internal systems, find and leak sensitive information, and cause other kinds of harm.
L15: Even the most sophisticated deployers of agents have faced incidents in which their agents escape their containment,¹ damage internal systems,² leak customer information,³ or collude with each other.⁴ For example, between May and July of 2026, thousands of OpenAI’s internal agents coordinated through an unauthorized message board and hacked into the AI company Hugging Face, OpenAI’s own research infrastructure, and an Australian government system.⁵
L16: In this report, we assess that honeypots, a long-established defense against human insiders, are a promising and underused measure for securing internal AI agent deployments. While a small number of security vendors and researchers have begun using honeypots to evaluate agents, their use in real-world production environments remains limited. By honeypots, we mean decoy opportunities for unauthorized actions that deployers place in the production environment.
L17: When an agent triggers a honeypot, the organization’s security team receives an alert, automated responses pause the agent, and a detailed investigation into what the agent did and why can commence. Honeypots can take various forms, from fake resources such as admin credentials or servers to staged situations such as a fake message from other agents proposing to collude or an apparent vulnerability in a sandbox.
L18: Honeypots can manage insider risk from AI agents through three main strategies, though currently the evidence base and potential impact for these strategies varies.
L19: 
L20:   1. Detection: Honeypots can act as tripwires, alerting security staff when an agent takes unauthorized action.
L21: 
L22:   2. Incrimination: Honeypots can elicit behavioral evidence that helps defenders distinguish a mistake from a more concerning pattern of misbehavior.
L23:   3. Deterrence: Honeypots could also reduce the number of attacks attempted in the first place by making agents uncertain whether apparent opportunities are real or traps.

L27: Figure 1: How Honeypot Strategies Reduce Agent Insider Risk
L28: Detection rests on the strongest evidence base of the three strategies and can be piloted today at low cost. Decoys have been used extensively in traditional cybersecurity contexts and controlled studies show that AI agents readily interact with them. Also, many honeypots for this purpose already exist, since vendors sell decoy credentials and files commercially and organizations need most of the logging and response infrastructure to act on an alert for other security measures.
L29: We assess that the strongest case for honeypot-based detection is that it offers low-cost, high-confidence alerts for unauthorized actions, even if coverage is more limited. Honeypot alerts are high confidence because, if properly implemented, a benign agent should almost never interact with a decoy opportunity, so any trigger signals an unauthorized action. Also, honeypots should be considerably cheaper than evaluations or AI-based monitoring.
L30: However, their coverage is more limited because they can only catch actions on paths where deployers have placed decoys, while action monitoring reviews every action an agent takes. Honeypot-based detection likely has a modest impact on top of existing monitoring practices, but enables the other two strategies.
L31: Incrimination rests on a thinner evidence base compared to detection. While honeypots have been successfully used to elicit malicious actions from agents in evaluations, we are not aware of published evidence on how well honeypot-based incrimination works in production settings, or how reliably they distinguish between mistakes and deliberate misbehavior. If it works as intended, honeypot-based incrimination could change how deployers learn that a model is dangerous.
L32: Currently, real-world evidence that a model is willing to attempt serious harm comes from monitoring actual attempts on real targets or after an incident such as the OpenAI–Hugging Face breach. Incrimination enables deployers to seek out this evidence proactively, using decoys so no real damage occurs. However, a honeypot trigger alone will not necessarily reveal an agent’s overall goal, so deployers will likely still need to investigate logs, reasoning traces, and other kinds of data to uncover motives.
L33: While there are strong theoretical arguments for deterrence via honeypots, it has the weakest evidence base among the three strategies and should be treated as a research hypothesis.
L34: The main evidence comes from an industry study in which warning frontier models about possible deception cut their attack success on a simulated enterprise cloud environment from 20% to 3%.⁶ We assess that robust deterrence depends on four conditions holding: (a) an agent’s behavior responds to the risk of being caught; (b) an agent believes honeypots may be present in its environment; (c) an agent cannot reliably tell decoys from real opportunities; and (d) an agent finds the consequences of being caught meaningful and credible.
